name: Jaisalmer
tagline: The golden fort-city rising from the Thar desert.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: October to February is the only comfortable window, and early February crowns it with the Desert Festival on the Sam dunes; avoid the extreme desert summer entirely.

ourTake.lede: Jaisalmer is the one living fort in India where people still reside inside the walls, so treat the citadel gently and consider staying in a restored haveli in town rather than inside the stressed fort itself. The point of coming is the desert; give a night to a proper dune camp away from the crowded Sam strip. Come in winter; the summer heat here is genuinely punishing.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a golden fort city and a night under the dunes in a luxury desert camp.
ourTake.skipIf: You want greenery, water or a fast pace.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Suryagarh Jaisalmer
items.area: Golden outskirts (Kahala Phata, ~15 min from the Fort)
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World, member property
Travel + Leisure India's Best Awards, recognised in Best Boutique Hotel category
items.description: A golden-sandstone fortress of its own making, the address Jaisalmer is measured against, and the keeper of the desert's rituals.

items.name: SUJÁN The Serai, Jaisalmer
credentials: Relais & Châteaux, member property
items.description: Canvas-tented suites on a hundred acres of private desert scrub, the caravan of Rajputana reimagined at the highest level.

items.name: Jaisalmer Marriott Resort & Spa
credentials: Marriott International, flagship resort property, Jaisalmer
items.description: A large, polished sandstone resort with the Golden Fort framed from the pool and the rooftop, international service, home-market ease.

items.name: Storii by ITC Hotels, Jaisalmer
credentials: ITC Hotels, Storii boutique portfolio
items.description: Havelis, jharokha balconies and chhatris across nine acres, ITC's boutique desert house, quietly grand.

items.name: WelcomHotel by ITC Hotels, Jaisalmer
credentials: ITC Hotels, WelcomHotel premium portfolio
items.description: ITC's premium desert house, the group's benchmark service in golden sandstone, without the icon's price.

items.name: Fort Rajwada
credentials: Rajasthan Tourism, recognised heritage-category five-star hotel
items.description: An early grand heritage-styled hotel of Jaisalmer, regal sandstone architecture and a long-established name in the city.

items.name: Jaisalmer Fort (Sonar Qila)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Hill Forts of Rajasthan
items.description: The world's only living fort still lived in, its yellow-sandstone bastions turning molten gold at dusk above the Thar. Roughly a quarter of the old city still resides inside its walls, so you walk through kitchens, temples and homes, not a museum piece.

items.name: Raj Mahal (Fort Palace Museum)
credentials: Inside UNESCO Hill Forts of Rajasthan WHS
items.description: The seven-storey royal palace of the Bhati rulers, now a museum of carved jharokhas, murals and the finest rooftop view over the golden warren of houses below. The private terraces where the Maharawals once took the desert air are the quiet showstopper.

items.name: Jain Temples inside the Fort
credentials: Inside UNESCO Hill Forts of Rajasthan WHS
items.description: A cluster of seven interconnected 12th–15th century Jain temples carved in honey sandstone, every pillar and ceiling a lace of dancers, animals and Tirthankaras. The cool, dim interiors are one of the most exquisite pieces of stonework in India.

items.name: Gyan Bhandar (Jain Manuscript Library)
items.description: An underground repository beneath the Jain temples holding palm-leaf manuscripts with painted wooden covers, some among the oldest surviving in India. A rare, hushed encounter with 11th-century Sanskrit and Prakrit texts most travellers never find.

items.name: Laxminath Temple
credentials: Inside UNESCO Hill Forts of Rajasthan WHS
items.description: The fort's principal Hindu shrine to Vishnu and Lakshmi, the spiritual heart the resident community still keeps alive with daily worship. Its silver-plated sanctum and morning aarti give a living contrast to the Jain temples nearby.

items.name: Patwon ki Haveli
items.description: A cluster of five mansions built by a wealthy brocade-and-opium merchant family, its facade a cascade of some sixty carved jharokhas, no two alike. The most opulent haveli in Jaisalmer and a masterclass in what desert stone can be coaxed to do.

items.name: Salim Singh ki Haveli
items.description: The mansion of a once-feared prime minister, crowned by a peacock-shaped upper storey that arches out over the street like a ship's stern. Its 38 balconies and top-heavy silhouette make it the most theatrical of the three great havelis.

items.name: Nathmal ki Haveli
items.description: Carved by two brothers working the left and right facades simultaneously, so the two halves are subtly, deliberately different. Life-size sandstone elephants flank the door, and the interiors still house the descendant family.

items.name: Gadisar Lake
items.description: A 14th-century rainwater reservoir ringed by ghats, temples and chhatris, entered through the ornate Tilon ki Pol gateway. A dawn boat glide here, with the fort catching first light behind you and migratory birds on the water, is Jaisalmer at its most serene.

items.name: Bada Bagh Cenotaphs
items.description: Rows of royal chhatris on a rise above a working windmill-dotted plain, the memorial garden of the Jaisalmer rulers. Come at sunset, when the domed cenotaphs glow amber and the desert light does the rest, one of the region's great photographic moments.

items.name: Vyas Chhatri (Sunset Point)
items.description: The Brahmin cremation ground of carved cenotaphs on a low hill, named for the sage Vyas, and the classic vantage for watching the sun drop behind the golden fort. Elegant, uncrowded and genuinely moving in the last light.

items.name: Sam Sand Dunes
items.description: The sweeping, postcard dunes of the Thar, where a camel or jeep safari at golden hour ends in a dune-top view of a horizon of pure sand. The heart of the desert-safari experience, and the setting for luxury camp nights under a vast sky.

items.name: Khuri Sand Dunes
items.description: A quieter, less-trafficked alternative to Sam, with softer dunes and a more intimate village-and-desert feel. The choice for travellers who want the silence of the Thar without the crowds, camel rides at dusk, then stars.

items.name: Luxury Desert Camp Night
items.description: A night in a canvas suite on the dunes, private butler, Marwari thali under the stars, a bonfire and folk performance, then silence. The signature multi-generational desert experience, with white-glove camps setting up bespoke on the sand.

items.name: Camel Safari on the Dunes
items.description: The traditional way to cross the Thar, swaying atop a camel as the light softens and the dunes ripple to the horizon. A short sunset ride suits families; longer dune-camp treks reward those who want the desert to unfold slowly.

items.name: Desert Jeep Safari
items.description: An open-jeep run over the crests and troughs of the dunes for those who want the desert with a jolt of adrenaline. Fast, exhilarating and an easy add-on before an evening at camp.

items.name: Kalbelia Dance & Manganiyar Music
credentials: Kalbelia folk songs & dances, UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage
items.description: The living folk heritage of the Thar, the sinuous Kalbelia gypsy dance and the haunting ballads of the hereditary Manganiyar musicians, performed by firelight. A private recital at a luxury camp is the finest way to hear it.

items.name: Desert Stargazing
items.description: Far from any city glow, the Thar's clear, dry skies deliver a canopy of stars few Indian destinations can match. Camps arrange telescopes and rooftop bedrolls; the Milky Way over the dunes is reason enough to stay the night.

items.name: Kuldhara Abandoned Village
items.description: The eerie ruins of a Paliwal Brahmin village abandoned overnight in the 19th century, its roofless sandstone homes now restored to a walkable ghost-town. A haunting, atmospheric detour steeped in legend and desert silence.

items.name: Khaba Fort
items.description: A small Paliwal-era fort on a rise above more abandoned village ruins, with a modest museum and sweeping desert panoramas. Pairs naturally with Kuldhara for a quieter, road-less-travelled morning.

items.name: Desert National Park & the Great Indian Bustard
credentials: Critically endangered Great Indian Bustard habitat
items.description: 3,000 sq km of dunes, salt flats and scrub protecting the critically endangered Great Indian Bustard, one of the last places on earth to see the giant bird in the wild. A guided jeep morning here rewards the patient birder and naturalist.

items.name: Tanot Mata Temple
items.description: The border shrine credited by soldiers with surviving hundreds of unexploded Pakistani shells in the 1965 and 1971 wars, now tended by the Border Security Force. Its Vijay Stambh and BSF-run devotion make it a stirring stop for the patriotically minded.

items.name: Longewala War Memorial
items.description: The site of the legendary 1971 stand where a small Indian post held off a Pakistani armoured column until the Air Force finished the job at dawn. Captured tanks and a memorial mark the ground, the story that inspired the film Border, seen where it happened.

items.name: Thar Heritage Museum
items.description: A one-man labour of love by folklorist Narayan Khatri, crammed with fossils, coins, manuscripts, instruments and the everyday objects of desert life. His personal, animated tours make it far richer than its modest size suggests.

items.name: Desert Culture Centre & Museum
items.description: A focused collection of Thar arts, crafts and folk instruments, with an evening puppet show that delights younger travellers. A tidy primer on Marwari desert culture before you head to the dunes.

items.name: Heritage Walk Through the Old City
items.description: A slow morning threading the sandstone lanes from Gandhi Chowk to the havelis and up into the fort, reading the carvings and the merchant history in the stone. The single best way to feel the Golden City rather than just tick its monuments.

items.name: Mirror-Work & Applique Artisan Quarter
items.description: The workshops where women stitch the mirror-embroidered, appliqued textiles the Thar is known for, cushion covers, wall hangings, quilts. A chance to buy directly from makers and understand the craft rather than the souvenir stall.

items.name: Camel-Leather Craft Workshops
items.description: Jaisalmer's distinctive embossed and painted camel-leather goods, jootis, bags, journals and lampshades, made in small family ateliers. A tactile, collectible craft rooted entirely in the desert economy.

items.name: Jaisalmer Stone Carving Ateliers
items.description: The workshops carrying on the sandstone-carving tradition that built the havelis, chiselling jaali screens and jharokhas by hand. Watching the craft that made the Golden City golden is a quiet highlight for the design-minded.

items.name: Lodhruva (Old Jain Capital)
items.description: The ancient Bhati capital before Jaisalmer, now a serene site whose exquisite Parshvanath Jain temple, celebrated Kalpavriksha wish-tree in carved metal and toran archway reward the journey. A tranquil, pilgrim-quiet counterpoint to the busy fort.

items.name: Amar Sagar & Jain Temple
items.description: A restored lake, garden and finely carved Jain temple complex on the road to Lodhruva, often combined with it. A calm, uncrowded stop that shows the Bhati taste for water and stone away from the crowds.

items.name: Akal Wood Fossil Park
credentials: National Geological Monument of India
items.description: A National Geological Monument where petrified tree trunks lie exactly where a tropical forest stood 180 million years ago, when the Thar was lush and coastal. A genuinely wondrous stop for curious families and the geologically inclined.

items.name: Pokhran Fort
items.description: The red-sandstone Bhati fort commanding the ancient caravan town, now a heritage stay and museum on the Jaisalmer–Jodhpur road. A worthwhile break with its own pottery tradition and the historical weight of the nearby nuclear-test region.

items.name: Ramdevra Temple (near Pokhran)
items.description: The revered shrine of the folk deity Baba Ramdevji, drawing pilgrims of every faith across western Rajasthan. An immersive, deeply local stop on the way to or from Jaisalmer for those who want faith beyond the monuments.

items.name: Suryagarh Jaisalmer
items.description: A fortress-like modern palace hotel that has become a destination in itself, known for curated experiences, dawn breakfasts in the dunes, Manganiyar concerts, secret desert dinners and the Thar's most refined table. The benchmark stay for UHNI travellers.

items.name: The Serai (Sujan)
items.description: A Relais & Chateaux tented camp of vast canvas suites and private pools set in a private desert reserve, the byword for barefoot luxury in the Thar. Sunset safaris, spa tents and starlit dining make it a stay rather than a base.

items.name: Sunset Camel Ride at Bada Bagh / Vyas Chhatri
items.description: A short, gentle camel amble along the ridges near the cenotaphs as the sun sets, the dunes' romance without the drive to Sam. An easy, evocative option for a first evening or for elders and children.

items.name: Jaisalmer Desert Festival (Maru Mahotsav)
items.description: The three-day February spectacle of camel races, turban-tying and moustache contests, folk music and a grand finale on the Sam dunes. The single most vivid window into Marwari desert culture, if your dates align.

items.name: Tazia Tower & Badal Mahal
items.description: A delicate five-tier pagoda-like tower built by Muslim craftsmen, rising beside the Badal Mahal palace outside the fort. An easily missed piece of Jaisalmer's syncretic artistry, best admired against a blue sky.

items.name: Fort Rooftop Café at Sunset
items.description: The rooftop cafés perched on the fort's edge offer a chai or thali with the whole golden city spilling below and the desert beyond. A relaxed, sociable way to watch the light change over Sonar Qila.

items.name: Gadisar to Fort Photography Walk (Golden Hour)
items.description: The angle every photographer chases, the fort mirrored in Gadisar's water at first or last light. A short, rewarding walk that captures why Jaisalmer earned the name Golden City.

items.name: Barmer & Balotra Textile Excursion
items.description: For the textile connoisseur, a longer excursion toward Barmer's block-printing and embroidery villages, a deeper dive into Marwari craft than the city bazaars offer. Best arranged privately with a craft-savvy guide.

items.name: Manganiyar & Langa Music Session (Private)
items.description: An arranged, intimate evening with the hereditary Langa and Manganiyar musicians whose ballads carry centuries of desert memory. Heard privately, away from the tourist show, it is one of the Thar's most soulful experiences.

items.name: Puppet Show (Kathputli)
items.description: The Rajasthani string-puppet tradition performed with quick wit and live music, a delight for multi-generational groups and children. A short, charming taste of Marwari folk theatre.

items.name: The Legend of Marwar (Suryagarh)
credentials: Inside Suryagarh Jaisalmer, Small Luxury Hotels of the World member; Travel + Leisure India's Best recognition
items.description: Royal Marwari fine dining inside the golden fortress, the grandest table in Jaisalmer, with music and dance under the stone.

items.name: The Serai, desert dining
credentials: Inside SUJÁN The Serai, Relais & Châteaux member property
items.description: Considered, seasonal cooking served in the tented mess or out on the dunes, dinner as theatre, on a private estate.

items.name: Desert Boy's Dhani
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India, featured Jaisalmer restaurant
items.description: A traditional dhani of thatched huts and low seating, with folk singers and dancers over a generous Rajasthani thali.

items.name: The Trio
items.area: Old City (Gandhi Chowk, near Amar Sagar Gate)
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India, featured Jaisalmer restaurant
items.description: The city's long-standing rooftop institution, tented ceilings, fort views and royal Rajasthani cooking with family warmth.

items.name: Saffron
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India, featured Jaisalmer restaurant
items.description: Refined rooftop dining above the lake, with the illuminated Fort as the backdrop and reinvented noble recipes on the plate.

items.name: Suryagarh bar & courtyard
credentials: Inside Suryagarh Jaisalmer, Small Luxury Hotels of the World member
items.description: A quiet drink in a lantern-lit sandstone courtyard, the most considered nightcap in the desert.

items.name: Rooftop bars & lounges, Old City
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India, Jaisalmer rooftop dining recognised
items.description: Sundowners on the fort-facing rooftops of the old town, the golden ramparts turning honey as the light goes.

items.name: Desert camp cultural evening (Sam / Khuri / private estates)
credentials: Signature Thar desert experience, Rajasthan Tourism
items.description: The true Jaisalmer night, Manganiyar folk musicians, fire and a canopy of stars over the dunes, drink in hand.

plan.heading: 3 days in Jaisalmer, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive at Suryagarh, the sandstone fort-hotel outside town, and rest through the midday sun.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A late-afternoon walk through the living Jaisalmer Fort and the carved Patwon-ki-Haveli with a guide.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Suryagarh's Legend of Marwad restaurant, with folk musicians in the courtyard.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A morning at the Gadisar Lake and the Jain temples inside the fort before the light climbs.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Rest, then a private jeep to the Sam or Khuri dunes, avoiding the camel-cart crowds.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A candlelit dinner set in the dunes by the hotel, under a full desert sky.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Ride out to the abandoned Kuldhara village and the chhatris at dawn, when the desert is coolest.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: An afternoon of textiles and a hammam-style spa treatment back at Suryagarh.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A last quiet dinner on the ramparts before onward travel.

items.name: Inside / just below the Sonar Fort
items.description: Amid the honey-coloured walls and havelis; best for those who want to live in the atmosphere.

items.name: Desert camps (beyond Sam/Khuri)
items.description: Out on the dunes under canvas; suits travellers who came for the Thar itself.

items.name: Town havelis (near Gadisar)
items.description: Restored merchant houses away from the fort crush; for a quieter, characterful base.

events.name: Jaisalmer Desert Festival
events.note: Three days of camel races, folk music and dune performances, culminating at Sam sand dunes.

events.name: Sindhu Darshan-region / cultural evenings
events.note: The cool months bring folk-music evenings in the havelis and forts across the season.

events.name: Holi
events.note: Celebrated with folk colour among the sandstone lanes, best experienced at a heritage haveli.

events.name: Diwali
events.note: The golden fort takes on the lamplight beautifully; a quiet, atmospheric time to visit.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Time your visit for the cool season (October to March); the desert is punishing in summer. A luxury tented camp with a private dune dinner is the signature experience, and the fort is one of the few still inhabited, so tread lightly.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Jaisalmer Airport (JSA) when the seasonal schedule allows, otherwise arrive by chauffeured car from Jodhpur (about five hours); a private car meets you and desert-camp operators handle the last leg to the dunes.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver for the fort and havelis, then on foot inside the living fort, and a 4x4 for the Sam and Khuri dunes.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: 4G holds in town but thins out in the deep desert; carry a preloaded Jio or Airtel eSIM and expect patchy signal at remote camps.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee (INR); carry more cash here than elsewhere, many haveli shops and camps prefer it, with 10 percent the tipping norm.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: November to February is the only comfortable window: warm days, cold desert nights, ideal for dunes and forts. Avoid April to June entirely, when the Thar exceeds 45C; the airport itself runs only in the cooler season.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Jaisalmer Airport (JSA) is seasonal, operating roughly October to March, with direct flights from Delhi and Mumbai (IndiGo, and Air India adding daily Mumbai from late October) plus links via Jaipur. Off-season, fly to Jodhpur and drive about 5 hours, or use the overnight train; arrange the car ahead, as the airport is bare-bones.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations beyond routine cover. Very safe. This is true desert: carry water, sun cover and warm layers for the night. Sealed water only.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Easy and vegetarian by default; Jain food is well understood in a Marwari desert town. The Suryagarh and Sujan The Serai kitchens do refined vegetarian menus; ker sangri, a desert-bean dish, is a local vegetarian specialty.
